analysis.investment_thesis: Borosil Renewables is India's sole domestic solar glass manufacturer — a compelling niche story in a genuine tailwind sector — but the story is broken: EBITDA collapsed from ₹256 Cr (FY22) to ₹73 Cr (FY25) even as revenue doubled, with net losses deepening to -₹87 Cr in FY25. At 73x P/E with negative earnings and a PEG that can't even be calculated, you're paying a premium for a deteriorating business.
key_strengths: Sole domestic manufacturer of solar glass — structural import-duty moat in a policy-protected sector
Revenue doubled from ₹642 Cr (FY22) to ₹1,476 Cr (FY25), confirming real demand growth
Conservative balance sheet: D/E of 0.23, borrowings sharply reduced from ₹576 Cr (FY24) to ₹203 Cr (FY25)
key_risks: Margin destruction is severe: Operating income fell from ₹223 Cr → ₹58 Cr while revenue doubled — Chinese glass competition is gutting pricing power
Net losses worsening consecutively: +₹166 Cr (FY22) → +₹71 Cr (FY23) → -₹50 Cr (FY24) → -₹87 Cr (FY25)
FCF negative in 4 of last 5 years (FY22: -₹200 Cr, FY23: -₹353 Cr, FY24: -₹148 Cr) with heavy capex cycle not yet yielding returns
red_flags: P/E of 73.3x with negative actual earnings — valuation is built on hope, not fundamentals
ROE -8.9% and ROCE -4.41%: capital is being destroyed, not compounded
Operating income flat at ₹58 Cr for two straight years (FY24/FY25) despite ₹1,400+ Cr revenue — scale is NOT helping margins
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From a Lynch perspective, I love the concept here — India's only solar glass maker, a clear niche monopoly you can observe from the country's massive solar buildout. That's exactly the kind of "invest in what you know" idea that gets me excited. But when I look under the hood, the numbers tell a horror story. Revenue growing from ₹891 Cr to ₹1,476 Cr over two years sounds terrific — until you see that operating income flatlined at ₹58 Cr both years and net losses are accelerating. That's the cardinal sin: revenue growth without profit growth means the business model is broken or the competitive moat has been breached. Chinese solar glass manufacturers are almost certainly the culprit, forcing prices down despite rising volumes.

The valuation makes no sense for a company losing money. A 73x P/E implies the market is pricing in a dramatic earnings recovery that isn't visible in the trajectory. The PEG ratio — my favorite metric — is incalculable because there are no positive earnings to divide into. Finance costs jumped from ₹6 Cr (FY19) to ₹32 Cr (FY25) as the company borrowed heavily to expand capacity (capex hit ₹373 Cr in FY22), yet that capacity hasn't translated into margin expansion. I'd classify this as a "turnaround" story at best, but turnarounds rarely turn. Pass until margins show two consecutive quarters of genuine recovery and the net loss reverses — at which point I'd want to see a much lower entry price.
